Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit.

We represent: defendant.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that shotgun pleadings that fail to give defendants adequate notice of the claims against them should be dismissed.

Cite at least six decisions of the Eleventh Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**I. The Complaint Is a Shotgun Pleading That Fails to Give Defendant Adequate Notice and Should Be Dismissed.**

Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 8(a)(2) requires "a short and plain statement of the claim showing that the pleader is entitled to relief." Rule 10(b) requires a party to state its claims "in numbered paragraphs, each limited as far as practicable to a single set of circumstances." Together, these rules require a complaint to give each defendant fair notice of what the claims are and the grounds on which they rest. This Court has long condemned complaints that do not meet that standard and has labeled them "shotgun pleadings." *See Weiland v. Palm Beach Cnty. Sheriff's Off.*, 792 F.3d 1313, 1320–23 (11th Cir. 2015); *Anderson v. Dist. Bd. of Trs. of Cent. Fla. Cmty. Coll.*, 77 F.3d 364, 366–67 (11th Cir. 1996).

**A. This Circuit's rule against shotgun pleadings.**

In *Weiland*, the Court surveyed its own case law and identified four rough types of shotgun pleading:

1. A complaint in which each count adopts the allegations of all preceding counts.
2. A complaint filled with conclusory, vague, and immaterial facts that are not tied to any particular cause of action.
3. A complaint that does not separate each cause of action into a different count.
4. A complaint that asserts multiple claims against multiple defendants without specifying which defendant is responsible for which acts.

792 F.3d at 1321–23. The Court explained that "[t]he unifying characteristic of all types of shotgun pleadings is that they fail to one degree or another, and in one way or another, to give the defendants adequate notice of the claims against them and the grounds upon which each claim rests." *Id.* at 1323. The Court has repeated that rule since. *See Vibe Micro, Inc. v. Shabanets*, 878 F.3d 1291, 1294–95 (11th Cir. 2018); *Jackson v. Bank of Am., N.A.*, 898 F.3d 1348, 1356–58 (11th Cir. 2018).

**B. The harm is to the defendant and to the court.**

A shotgun pleading forces the defendant to guess which allegations support which claims. It makes a meaningful responsive pleading impossible. A defendant cannot admit or deny allegations, assert targeted defenses, or frame discovery when it cannot tell what it is accused of doing. *See Anderson*, 77 F.3d at 366–67. The harm extends to the judicial system. This Court has said that shotgun pleadings "wreak havoc on the judicial system" and divert resources from the dockets of litigants with well-pleaded claims. *See Davis v. Coca-Cola Bottling Co. Consol.*, 516 F.3d 955, 979 & n.54 (11th Cir. 2008); *Cramer v. Florida*, 117 F.3d 1258, 1263 (11th Cir. 1997). Where a complaint is so unclear that the court cannot readily determine which facts support which claims, the court should not have to sort through it. *See Magluta v. Samples*, 256 F.3d 1282, 1284 (11th Cir. 2001) (per curiam) (describing the district court's burden in handling a complaint of this kind).

**C. The Complaint falls within the prohibited categories.**

The Complaint fits the first, third, and fourth *Weiland* categories. [Describe: each count incorporates by reference all preceding paragraphs and counts, so that later counts carry forward the legal conclusions of earlier ones. Cite Compl. ¶¶ __.] Several counts also combine distinct causes of action, or distinct theories of liability, in a single count. [Cite Compl. Counts __.] The Complaint also groups multiple defendants together and attributes conduct to "Defendants" collectively. It does not say which defendant did what, or which claim is asserted against which defendant. [Cite Compl. ¶¶ __.] That kind of group pleading is the problem *Weiland* identified in its fourth category. 792 F.3d at 1323. Defendant cannot tell which of the allegations concern it, or what conduct it must answer for. *Cf. Strategic Income Fund, L.L.C. v. Spear, Leeds & Kellogg Corp.*, 305 F.3d 1293, 1295 & n.9 (11th Cir. 2002) (criticizing the practice of incorporating all prior allegations into each count).

**D. Dismissal is the appropriate remedy.**

District courts have the inherent authority to control their dockets and to dismiss a shotgun pleading. *Vibe Micro*, 878 F.3d at 1295. When a plaintiff files a shotgun pleading, the court should give the plaintiff at least one chance to replead. *Id.* A defendant may seek dismissal under Rule 12(b)(6), or may seek a more definite statement under Rule 12(e). *See Jackson*, 898 F.3d at 1357–58. The Court should dismiss the Complaint. It should require Plaintiff to file an amended pleading that (1) does not incorporate prior counts wholesale, (2) pleads each cause of action in a separate count, and (3) states which defendant is responsible for which acts. Because Plaintiff has already been put on notice of these defects, [if applicable: and has failed to cure them in a prior pleading,] dismissal with prejudice is warranted. *See Vibe Micro*, 878 F.3d at 1295–96.
